processing: Mainly steamed sencha; the cultivar also suits shaded kabusecha and gyokuro.
harvest_season: Spring. It buds early, about two to three days ahead of Yabukita.
appearance_dry: Bright green needles when made as sencha.
appearance_liquor: Clear, bright yellow-green, as is usual for a sencha of this colour.
appearance_wet: Soft, vivid green leaf, as is typical of steamed tea.
taste_profile: Strong umami with low bitterness and astringency, refreshing, with aroma notes of peach and chestnut.

brewing.notes: Standard sencha parameters, on the cooler side to bring out the umami. For a shaded version go cooler still.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, like other Japanese greens, usually as a named single-cultivar sencha from small gardens. Because it picks early, it can reach the market as an early new-season tea. Drink within about a year.
description:
Kirari 31 is one of the newer Japanese cultivars, bred in Miyazaki and aimed squarely at the modern taste for sweet, savoury green tea. The name plays on words: kirari is a flash of light, and 31 reads as san (sun) and ippai (plenty).

It comes from a cross of Sakimidori and Saemidori. It yields well, runs high in amino acids and low in tannin, which is what you want for umami. Makers use it for sencha, and it also takes well to shading for kabusecha and gyokuro.

Expect a rich, clean cup with little bitterness, and a fruity-nutty aroma often described as peach and chestnut. Because the leaf is so naturally savoury, cooler water pays off; too hot and you lose the point of the cultivar.

Look for it as a single-cultivar lot from Kyushu, such as Yame. A side-by-side with Saemidori, one of its parents, is a good way to see what the breeding achieved.
history:
The cross was made in 1994 at the tea branch of Miyazaki Prefecture's agricultural experiment station, with the best seedling selected with trials recorded in 1999 and 2004. Registration under the Seed and Seedling Law came in the mid-2010s; 2015 and 2016 are both given.

The cultivar has since been trialled in other prefectures, including Nagasaki, where it out-yielded Yabukita.
